1.0.13 (build 4694)   Nov 16, 2026   This version

New: Tour into the picture

  • One still becomes a room the camera moves through. Projection has a new mode for a single picture, Tour into the picture: right-click a still in the Viewer and choose Tour into this picture, or add a Projection to a still. Five steps, shown on the Viewer's bar and free to jump between: Picture, Room, Things, Fill and Move. Next always names the next thing to do.
  • Room: the room is found from the picture's own straight edges, as the Perspective node finds lines, and drawn over the still at once as a first guess you correct. Drag where the lines meet, a corner of the back wall, or a line's end onto an edge in the picture. A solved Perspective node up the still can seed the room and its lens instead. Click two points and type how long they are to give the room a real size, in meters or feet.
  • Things: click round a thing and it stands where its foot touches, on the floor, hanging from the ceiling or out of a wall. Drag its foot nearer or farther and its top for its height, stand one thing on another, or make one from a Roto shape or a node's alpha.
  • Fill: what the still never showed (behind each thing, and past the picture's edges) is hatched and filled from the pixels around it, so a move that drifts past the edge sees picture, not black. When the room or a thing moves afterward, Fill says it is out of date and offers Fill again.
  • Move: presets named by situation, sliders for push in, drift, rise, turn, tilt, orbit and lens, a map of the room from above, and flying in the Viewer. When the move would see what the picture never showed, a card says where and offers Fill it or Limit the move. Out gives the moving picture at the comp's format; for 3D work, the camera, the room's lines as a Perspective node, and the room and its things as USD or Alembic. In a Nuke script it's offered for baking, with Nuke cameras.

    • New: guided steps on 27 tools

  • Kento's more involved tools now open on a few short steps instead of every control at once. A strip at the top of the panel shows where you are; each step says in one line what to do and shows only its own controls, and Next names the step it goes to. When a step can't go on, an amber line says why with the one button that fixes it ("Couldn't measure: A has too little solid matte", Measure again), and the Viewer's top left shows the same words.
  • All controls, at the strip's right, shows the whole panel as before, with the steps folded above it. Kento remembers your choice for each kind of node, so an artist who knows a tool keeps the full panel.
  • With steps: SmartMerge, HeatHaze, Perspective, Furea, Kiri, ReadSplat, PlateAlign, Grain Match, Nagi, Lens Defocus, DepthGenerator, Isolate, the Lens node, Trainer, RemoveGlare, Matte Refine, ScannedGrain, Clean Plate, MultiMerge, Frame Repair, Position Matte, Create LUT, Prerender, RemoveFlare, Generate and TextureFill. Paint gets a short start checklist instead (what you're painting, the clone source, this frame or every frame) that folds away after the first stroke.
  • A ReadSplat take (a sequence or moving splats) has two more steps once it's in the shot: Playback and Prerender.
  • Perspective's last step, Use, is optional: once the solve is good the panel opens folded to Done.
  • Steps put the right tool in your hand: HeatHaze opens on the Jet or car exhaust preset with the point tool on, so one click where the heat comes from is enough; Perspective's line tool moves to the other direction by itself after two lines; Clean Plate starts with the screen pick on and warns that the default green turns a non-green plate black.
  • A step that needs something else makes it there: Grain Match's Clean step adds a Nagi set up for you, and Lens Defocus's Depth step adds a DepthGenerator, each with its own steps running inside. Steps that need a download (SAM 3.1, the depth, matte and flare models) say so first, with the size, and show the download's progress beside Cancel.
  • Long jobs run in the background with their progress beside Stop: PlateAlign's Track and solve and Align, Kiri's Work out the shot (frames counted, with the time left), Matte Refine, DepthGenerator and RemoveFlare. RemoveFlare, Matte Refine and DepthGenerator show a shot's results when it finishes even if their panel was closed.
  • A click on the picture while a step's tool is on and the Viewer shows another node is refused where you clicked, in a card that fades by itself, with the button that shows the right node.
  • Walking every tool step by step turned up quiet failures, now fixed: Perspective's Camera step asks for the film back (it was folded away, so the focal length came out wrong on most plates without a word); leaving Kiri's Check step puts the Viewer back on Result, so a Matte or Spill view never reaches a render; Create LUT no longer writes a LUT that would change nothing, asks before writing over a file it didn't write, and no longer leaves a Blur switched off after leaving it out of a LUT; ReadSplat's Put in the shot waits for a line-up (it built a network that couldn't line up); the Lens node's lens grid no longer picks the plate itself as the grid; Isolate says when the playhead is outside the tracked frames; Frame Repair says when a word in its list isn't a frame; Prerender's buttons say why they can't start by the button instead of in a dialog.

    • New: buttons you can see

  • Every word you can press (Go to hold, Hold here, Send to paint, Add track, Skip This Version and about 330 more) now has a raised face with a fine light top edge, so it is no longer a guess which words do something. A row's main action is light, ringed in blue; a switch that is on is sunk and lighter; a button that can't be pressed yet keeps its shape, faint. Information, such as a state or a count, stays flat and round. Projection's Best hold... is its row's main action.

    • New: Furea, a flare built from elements

  • Furea's flare is now one stack of elements: the light's core, the iris star, the glow, the veil, the horizontal streak, ghosts traced through a lens, lit dirt, and the rings, iris ghosts, ghost chains and haze you add. Each has its own strength, color, solo, layer and seed, and traced ghosts and drawn ghosts sit in the same flare. A comp saved with an earlier Furea opens as its stack and renders the same.
  • Each element has looks, each a different structure rather than a different strength (the Core's Pinpoint, Sun disc, Lamp and Blown out, for one), measured against the studio's anamorphic and spherical flare footage and reference photographs of its kind of lens. The horizontal streak looks are now the coating's blue rather than white, fading and tapering along their length as real streaks do. Nine new elements: Fine rays, Streak glints, Star filter, Rainbow arc, Tall oval ghost, Lens orbs, Glare rays, Dust specks and Scratches.
  • The twenty presets are now starter flares you can change, and a new Furea opens on the flare you used last. Save flare keeps one for you with its group, tags and a thumbnail; adding it to the studio's library is a separate step that asks what it is for, and the library shows who added each flare and when.
  • The panel is built around the stack: Start from (starters, yours and the studio's, searchable), Light, Whole flare (scale, strength, squeeze, lens, irregularity, flicker), the Elements list (show, solo, strength and drag to reorder on each row) and the chosen element's own rows. In the Viewer, each element has a mark you can drag along the line through the frame's center, and Flare, Solo element and Elements outlined switch what you see.
  • The light is a Point you place in the Viewer, key, or link to a Tracker's track or a CameraTracker's point, or Hotspots found in the picture. Hotspots can merge lights close together into one and cap any one light, so one sun doesn't drown every other light's flare; when no light is as bright as it asks, it lowers the threshold to the brightest light and says so.
  • Traced ghosts can trace a lens of their own (design, focal length and stop) beside the whole flare's, so two lenses' ghosts sit in one flare. List... shows each ghost, brightest first: hide one, or turn it into an Iris ghost you can move freely.

    • Faster

  • A Write no longer waits for movie frames it never uses: Kento decodes a movie's frame only when the render reads its pixels. On a 4.6K comp with a retimed 4K ProRes smoke element (DNK_320), the matte Write beside it went from 0.40 to about 0.20 seconds a frame on a Mac Studio, and the comp's three benchmark Writes now render faster than NukeX 17.1's on the same machine. Writes that do show the movie still have its frames decoded ahead. The pixels are exactly the same.

    • New: AVIF, HEIC and WebP stills

  • A Read opens AVIF, HEIC and WebP stills. On the Mac, macOS's own decoders read them. Wide-gamut photos (Display P3 from a phone) and HDR photos (PQ, HLG, an iPhone photo's HDR rendition) keep their own colors as linear float, read through the config's linear Rec.709 space, so nothing clips; sRGB files read as they are and 10-bit files keep their precision; transparency comes in as a PNG's does, and a photo taken sideways stands upright. The Read's metadata says the file's format, bit depth and profile. Drag them onto the Node Graph, choose them in the file dialog or as Tour into the picture's still, and see them in the Browser's thumbnails. On Windows and Linux, WebP reads; AVIF and HEIC don't yet.

    • Better

  • .ko files show Kento's icon in the Finder instead of a page of text, and double-clicking one opens the Kento you are running, including after an update.
  • A node's button that can't do what was asked now says why in a card under the button that fades by itself, instead of a tip that vanished as the pointer moved: Grain Match's Analyze, Lens Defocus's pick and the other node buttons. TextureFill's Keep after a bake says what it kept, or why it couldn't.
  • Nagi's Auto Setup, Lock and Move to flat say why when there is nothing to measure, and Lock goes back to off instead of staying lit. DepthGenerator, RemoveFlare and Matte Refine say by the button when a run can't start.
  • Matte Refine with nothing on its matte input says "No matte connected" under the matte row, instead of a black picture with no word. RemoveGlare's soft flare rebuilt from a clean plate with none wired says so, with Use the surroundings beside it.
  • A Projection on a still shows the picture while there is nothing to project yet (no camera, or no plane drawn), so the plane's corners can be clicked on it; the Viewer's row says why, with a Draw a plane button. Drawing a plane switches the Viewer to the Projection when it shows another node, and the first click on the picture starts the plane. Room from one vanishing point is in the Projection's onto menu and the Viewer's menu.
  • The plane tool's hint in the Viewer is one short line. A wall drawn square on points to Room from one vanishing point instead of asking for a camera, and Camera from this plane puts the new camera beside the Projection in the Node Graph.

    • Fixed

  • Furea's traced ghosts in Draft and Good are closer to Final's brightness: Draft and Good trace three wavelengths to Final's seven, and each ghost's light is now scaled to what Final's seven carry through its lens coatings (Good's ghosts differ from Final's by 2.7% on average, from 8.1%). They don't match Final yet: Draft's coarser ray grid still draws some big ghosts up to about 1.5 times brighter. Final renders exactly as before.
  • ScanlineRender2's panel no longer shows two tabs named ScanlineRender: its splat rows join its own tab.
  • Fixed a crash after many node panels had been opened and closed, in a timer of the scan that marks nodes switched off and boxes that grow.
  • SmartMerge's Automatic now measures a SmartMerge added to an open comp; it only did so for comps opened with the SmartMerge already in them. A measure that fails says why and no longer claims a match.
  • Kiri's Click the subject keeps the key until a subject is clicked, and works from inside Kiri.
  • The Lens node's Fixed and Refine are back on every value tracking gets (only distortion had them). Trainer's Find fixed frames and Paint a fix keep their result on screen instead of clearing it at once. Isolate's setup hint names the right Settings page (AI and MCP).

    • Earlier updates

    1.0.12 (build 4604)   Nov 15, 2026

    Faster

  • A row of Keymixes, as in a defocus made of slices, renders in one pass instead of one pass and a copy for each, and is kept between frames when it doesn't change: MM1_080's main Write renders in about 0.59 s a frame instead of 0.67 on the Mac Studio, the same pixels.
  • RemoveGlare is faster, most with Richardson-Lucy: about a third less time a 4K frame (3.1 to 2.1 s on a busy MacBook Pro), the same picture.
  • Dragging a knob on a heavy comp shows the picture as you drag: the Viewer finishes each picture before it takes the next value, instead of starting over at every move and showing nothing until you let go (POP_010 on a 16 GB Mac mini: no picture during a drag before, one every 1.7 to 2.5 seconds now, about one a second at 1:2). Letting go sets the last value at once.
  • On a Mac with 16 GB of memory or less, Kento starts with smaller caches (image cache 4 GB, playback cache 2 GB), so a long session leaves room for your other apps: on a 16 GB Mac mini a session held about 3 GB less. Settings > Performance shows and changes them as before.
  • Clicking a node in a big comp opens its panel sooner: the Properties panels no longer restyle every open panel at each selection (POP_010 on a 16 GB Mac mini: a click to its panel about 0.8 s before, 0.5 s now).
  • Clicking a knob or stepping to another frame while the Viewer is still working out a big comp's picture no longer freezes the interface until that picture is done: the render engine stops the picture you moved on from at once (POP_010 on a 16 GB Mac mini: a frame step mid-picture held the interface about 1.3 s before, 0.1 s now; a knob click 0.7 s before, 0.06 s now).
  • Stepping through frames the Viewer has already worked out no longer holds up the interface on a big comp: read ahead no longer searches the whole comp at every frame, the Timeline works out its range once a paint, and a Read asks whether its EXR sequence is deep once instead of reading every frame's header (POP_010 on a 16 GB Mac mini: the interface's own time for a step about 0.6 s before, 0.3 s now).
  • Rendering an image sequence, the nodes after a Read no longer work out the picture's size, bounding box and channels again at each new frame when the files' headers are the same: MND_040's main Write gets each frame ready about 0.12 s sooner (0.65 to 0.54 s), the same files.
  • EXR files are written faster: each frame's file is compressed across all of the machine's cores and written in order as its parts are done, and up to three files are written while the next Writes render, so a Write that only copies a plate no longer waits for the file before it (a 4.6K plate copy about 0.08 s to 0.055 s a frame), the same files.
  • A big comp gets each frame ready for the render in about half the time: the parts of a frame's plan that are the same as the frame before are no longer written out and read back again (MND_040's main Write, 1,244 nodes: about 1.4 s to 0.8 s a frame on a busy Mac Studio), the same files.
  • Opening a Nuke script is faster again: each Merge is now one node inside Kento instead of about 45, with the same pixels and the same saved scripts, so a comp with hundreds of Merges opens faster (POP_010 in 1.5 s instead of 3.0 on the Mac Studio, a 1,000-node comp in 1.75 s instead of 2.16). A Keymix is now one node too, and Merges with a driven inject or mix stay one node. A Read, Grade or ColorCorrect builds its view, missing-frame and mix luminance parts only when they are used. A Read is ten nodes lighter inside again, with the same pictures.
  • A run of Grades, Multiplys, Expressions, Clamps, Shuffles, channel copies and matte merges one after another is worked out in one pass on the GPU on a Mac instead of one pass a node, with the same pixels: the ten nodes of an edge-push matte become one, and so do the fifteen of two ChannelMerges with the Invert and Shuffle after them.
  • An Erode (filter) or an EdgeExtend works out only the channels the nodes after it read (an EdgeExtend whose color nothing reads does no fill), a Transform left at its defaults passes its picture through, and a Merge of pictures with different bounding boxes no longer slows down outside the smaller one: a 4K comp that builds an edge matte from a lightwrap (two erodes of its alpha) renders that matte in about a third of the time.
  • Opening a big Nuke script is faster: an expression's text is read once however many nodes share it, and a node's mask and mix are set up only once it is masked or mixed, so a 1,000-node comp opens in about 2.5 s instead of 3.5 on the Mac Studio, the same comp.
  • On a Mac with 48 GB of memory or more, a long render keeps more of its working memory between frames (up to a quarter of the machine's memory, at most 24 GB) instead of asking the system for it again each frame: a heavy 4K comp renders its frames about a quarter faster after the first.
    • A comp whose Writes share most of their nodes (one Write a shuffle or crop of another's picture) works those nodes out once a frame, not once a Write: DNK_100's second Write takes about 0.15 s a frame instead of 0.45, the same files.
    • A Reformat that neither scales nor moves its input (to the format the picture already has, resize none) passes the picture through instead of filtering it: POP_010's 37-channel render passes no longer spend an eighth of a second each on it, the same picture.
    • A Keymix (or any masked node) whose mask is a roto works out its A input only where the mask is above zero, not over the whole frame: PR1_120, whose rotating wheels are motion-blurred Transforms of the 4K plate under small rotos, renders a frame in about 0.15 s instead of 0.8 on the Mac Studio, the same picture.
    • Layered Photoshop files and other decoded copies (PNG, movie frames) are read once per render instead of on every frame, and a masked node reads only its mask's channel: a 4K comp with a layered matte painting and a ProRes movie renders about 1.8 times as fast, the same to the bit.
    • H.264 and HEVC movies decode on the Mac's media engines (VideoToolbox), the same pixels as before; ProRes already decodes there.
    • A ProRes movie Read keeps its decoder open between frames and unpacks frames on every core: a render of frames far apart prepares each new frame's movie frames in about half the time (0.27 s instead of 0.4 for four 4K frames on the Mac Studio), the same pixels.
    • Movie Writes keep the timecode of their first frame (from a Read or AddTimeCode) as a timecode track, as other apps write it.
    • Movie Writes and QuickTime flipbooks encode on the Mac's media engines and prepare their frames on every core: a 4K Write of 24 frames takes 6.6 s instead of 38 in ProRes 4444, and 3.1 s instead of 25 in H.264, with the same codec, profile and color tags.
    • Convolve with an even-sized filter (a Radial or Constant 162 pixels wide, say) now runs on the GPU too: it fell back to the slowest way, about 3 seconds a 4K frame, and now takes about a tenth of a second.
    • Big blurs and their reduced copies use the GPU and every core more often (blurs of 31 taps and up, pictures with values below zero, and the shrink and grow steps of very large blurs), with the same picture as before.
    • Expression nodes run on the GPU on a Mac where they can (color math, comparisons, gammas, clamps; not positions or angles, which keep the CPU's precision).
    • Very large blurs (past their quality) shrink, blur and grow their copy on the GPU on a Mac in one go, the shrunk copy never leaving the GPU; the picture is the same but for an odd value one float step apart.
    • Colorspace to and from CIE-LCH, CIE-Lab and CIE-XYZ (the Photoshop-style blend modes in PSDMerge use them) runs on the GPU on a Mac: a 4K comp with PSDMerge renders about a third faster.
    • PNG Reads with alpha (roto mattes) no longer copy each frame to a temporary TIFF while rendering: the renderer reads the PNG itself, the same picture to the bit. A 4K comp with four roto PNGs renders about 0.15 s a frame faster.
    • A Transform with motion blur sums its samples in one pass on the GPU instead of making a full picture for each: about twice as fast on a 4K plate, the same picture to the bit.
    • Turned and scaled Transforms run on the GPU on a Mac, the same picture to the bit, and motion blur sums its samples faster: a 4K Transform with motion blur renders in about 0.18 s instead of 0.25.
    • EdgeExtend fills on the GPU on a Mac, the same picture to the bit: a 4K EdgeExtend takes about a twentieth of a second instead of a quarter.
    • OCIODisplay, OCIOColorSpace and other OCIO color conversions run on the GPU on a Mac (OCIO's own shader for the conversion, within a half float's step of the CPU's numbers; conversions that use LUT files stay on the CPU for now): a 4K display conversion takes a few milliseconds instead of a tenth of a second.
    • A render reuses what it prepared for frames a comp holds (FrameHold, a held 3D setup) instead of preparing it again on every frame, and prepares the next frame on the Mac's fast cores: MND_040 prepares a frame in about 0.6 s instead of 1.0, the same picture to the bit.
    • 3D scenes hand their triangles to the renderer as packed numbers instead of text: a tracked-geometry comp (MND_040) spends about a third of a second less on each frame, the same picture to the bit.
    • A ReadGeo mesh with its own normals is read in a blink instead of seconds a frame: a 4K comp with tracked 3D geometry (MND_040) prepares each frame about 3 times as fast, the same picture to the bit.
    • ColorCorrect runs on the GPU on a Mac, Grade (the Gaffer kind inside many tools) reads its rows straight, and Erode (filter) uses the GPU for a part of the picture too: a heavy 4K comp such as DNK_320 renders about a fifth faster.

    New

  • Kento seats render for each other on the studio's Tailscale network: each Kento finds the others by itself and lists them in Settings > Rendering and on the Render Queue's new seats line as available, busy, in use or asleep, with no node list to fill in. A new Gently, while I work setting keeps a seat rendering while its artist works, with a few threads, a small cache, low priority and no GPU, and at full speed once they're away; idle now counts the mouse, keys and pen in any app, not only Kento's window.
  • Gaussian splats in the 3D (3D > Geometry > ReadSplat): a splat capture (PLY from a splat trainer, SPZ or .splat) is drawn by ScanlineRender through the comp's camera, on the GPU on a Mac, in depth with cards and meshes and in the Z pass, and shows as colored points in the 3D Viewer.
  • ReadSplat reads splats over time: a take of numbered splat frames (PLY, SPZ, .splat, SOG) conformed to the comp's rate with start at and offset, nearest or held frames, missing frames filled, a read-ahead that follows the playhead within a quarter of the memory free and a half-size frame cache, a frames strip and Timeline band showing what's in memory, and Prerender for playback for smooth review; moving-splat files (.splatv, Spacetime Gaussians PLY) play exactly at any time with real motion blur and their own motion in ScanlineRender's motion vectors, and several can be segments of one take, each segment's numbers keyable.
  • PlateAlign (Transform > Tracking): lines up a take that should have been shot motion control with the master take. Track each plate with its CameraTracker and press Align: the child is lined up in space (from the points both plates show, or the turn alone for cameras on sticks), retimed so each master frame shows its nearest moment, drawn through the master's camera, and each frame's error is graphed. Bake makes a TimeWarp and a CornerPin2D for Nuke.
  • ReadSplat puts a splat capture in the shot: presets for the kind of shot (Phone scan cleanup, Set extension behind the action, Quick layout and more); Keep and Crop drop faint, oversized and floating splats or cap their count, and crop to a box or sphere dragged in the 3D Viewer; Line up fits the cloud to a solved CameraTracker by the points both share or by pairs you pick; scale, ground and origin give the shot its real size; Put in the shot makes the Scene, the render through the tracked camera and the Merge over the plate in one click. Splats are turned from sRGB into the working space, can be drawn as themselves in the 3D Viewer, and ScanlineRender can write them alone to their own layer. Came from names the capture tools (XGrids PortalCam, Nerfstudio, Scaniverse, Postshot and more) and sets their axis; a PortalCam capture's levels and sky are offered, and its cameras.json comes in as Cameras.
  • Lens Defocus (Filter > Blur and defocus): depth defocus with a real lens's bokeh, bright rims in front of focus, cat's eyes toward the frame's edges, color fringes, swirl and anamorphic ovals, from four looks traced from real lenses, with a preview of the bokeh across the frame, Pick in Viewer for the focus, and focus breathing. With DepthGenerator or a render's Z pass; on the GPU.
  • HeatHaze (Filter): heat haze and steam from a simulated flow of hot air, not a noise warp. Pick a preset (hot road, exhaust, fire, desert, candle, steam vent, kettle, manhole steam) and show it the source: a matte, emitters drawn in the Viewer, or the plate's bright areas. Plumes rise, curl and flow around solid things; a depth pass keeps nearer things still. Its outputs: the finished image, an STMap and the steam's density.
  • RemoveGlare (Filter): takes veiling glare, soft flare and haze, and streaks out of a plate. Pick a light and its glare's falloff is drawn with the spread fitted to it (drag the curve's end to widen or narrow it); soft flare is rebuilt from the surroundings, a clean plate or the neighboring frames, the grain kept; streaks are turned on a dial. Removed shows what was taken out, Before and after splits the picture at a line you drag in the Viewer.
  • Furea (Beta: results vary), a lens flare worked out from a lens (Filter > Light and glow): ghosts traced through the glass, a starburst from the iris, veiling glare and dirt on the front glass, with the imperfections a real lens has, set off by a point, a 3D light or the plate's highlights, on the GPU; Designer mode builds one from elements.
  • Furea's presets are temporary (beta): they don't match real flares closely enough yet, and an element library you stack into a flare will replace them in a later Kento. Furea's presets (board 184, revised 15 Nov): one Preset menu of twenty looks in five groups (Daylight, modern glass; Vintage and worn; Anamorphic; Night and practical lights; Graphic and stylized), each a different lens, coating, stop or streak, your own at the foot; Light keeps the preset's optics; Strength (Subtle, Natural, Bold) in place of the Lens type and Genre menus, an old comp's genre shown as its strength. The lens menu is searchable and lists Kento's designs and lenses imported as .lens files (FlareSim's format) into the studio's Furea lens library (Import .lens files...). The star follows the stop; the anamorphic streak's thickness, edges, halo, lines, length and color are controls.
  • Annotations: draw on the Viewer (pen, line, arrow, box, ellipse, text, in seven colors) on one frame or held across a range, with a line of words; they are saved with the comp, show on the Timeline, never reach a render, and go to and from Asobi (a file, its review window) and the shot's Kitsu notes. Bar 2's Annotations button.
  • Annotations read from the shot's Kitsu notes open their Kitsu picture: More > Exchange with Asobi... > Open this annotation's Kitsu picture.
  • A loupe and a navigator in the Viewer: bar 2's loupe button shows the pixels under the pointer enlarged, with their values, and the navigator shows where a zoomed-in view sits in the frame (click or drag in it to move there).
  • Gamut scopes: the Scopes panel adds CIE xy and a gamut view with the working, display and one more gamut drawn, counts the pixels outside the display, and a click on that count marks them in the Viewer.
  • RemoveFlare (Filter, beta: results vary; RemoveGlare for dependable removal): takes a lens flare's ghosts and streaks out of a plate with a learned model (Flare7K++ or FlareX, installed from the panel). Work out the shot once; only the flare is taken from the full-size plate, so grain stays, smoothed across frames so it doesn't flicker, and a farm renders it with no model. Removed shows what was taken; a matte on where keeps it to the flare.
  • DepthGenerator (Other > Models): a depth channel for any plate from a learned model, no camera needed. Work out the shot once, steady across the shot or a frame at a time; near, far and depth (1/z) or distance (z) change instantly, and the farm renders it with no model. The models install from its panel or Settings > AI and MCP > Depth model (about 340 MB on a Mac).
  • Matte Refine has a third solve, learned: a learned model (ViTMatte Small or Base, BiRefNet matting, MatAnyone 2 for steady video, or BackgroundMattingV2 against a clean plate) turns a rough roto or key into an alpha with the hair and edge detail, worked out over the shot in the background and kept beside the comp. Its models install from the panel or Settings > AI and MCP > Matting models (about 1.9 GB on a Mac).
  • SmartMerge as a balancer: set result to A matched to B and it gives you the element matched to the plate (levels, color, haze, grain, defocus), premultiplied by its own alpha and not merged, to comp yourself, or to match one CG pass or plate to another. The plate is still what it measures. Light wrap and the operation dim with the reason (the wrap needs the plate behind), mix blends with the element as it came, its tile says "matched only", and Bake to nodes and a saved .nk follow it with no Merge. Tab finds it by "match to plate".

    • Fixed

  • Furea: a light is a crisp core with its rays, streak and ghosts, not a soft round halo. The halo close round a light (the bloom and the near part of the veil) is one control, glow, with glow size, low by default (a quarter of what it was) and up for a glowing look; Sci-fi streak and Energy orb keep theirs. An anamorphic's bloom is small and faint (2 to 3% of the frame's height) and follows the glow. No ghost reads as a second source: ghosts fade out beside the light they come from and stay soft round it; an uncoated lens's are fainter and smaller. Each light gets its own long rays on an anamorphic (never one pattern copied). 1970s single-coated and Sodium street lights throw less ghost wash.
  • Furea's anamorphic presets, from the studio's anamorphic flare footage: a cyan bloom round the core (6 to 8% of the frame's height), a near-vertical spike and one long diagonal ray through the light (uneven, each way its own length), and a wide faint elliptical ring ghost with a rainbow rim across the frame's center from the light. An uncoated lens's ghosts are soft, warm and low in contrast (no hard white disc beside the light); Stage lights in haze no longer shows green smears.
